sections.heading: Abstract
sections.content: Large Language Model (LLM) agents demonstrate strong performance in autonomous code generation under loose specifications. However, production-grade software requires strict adherence to structural constraints, such as architectural patterns, databases, and object-relational mappings. Existing benchmarks often overlook these non-functional requirements, rewarding functionally correct but structurally arbitrary solutions. We present a systematic study evaluating how well agents handle structural constraints in multi-file backend generation. By fixing a unified API contract across 80 greenfield generation tasks and 20 featureimplementation tasks spanning eight web frameworks, we isolate the effect of structural complexity using a dual evaluation with end-to-end behavioral tests and static verifiers. Our findings reveal a phenomenon of constraint decay: as structural requirements accumulate, agent performance exhibits a substantial decline. Capable configurations lose 30 points on average in assertion pass rates from baseline to fully specified tasks, while some weaker configurations approach zero. Framework sensitivity analysis exposes significant performance disparities: agents succeed in minimal, explicit frameworks (e.g., Flask) but perform substantially worse on average in convention-heavy environments (e.g., FastAPI, Django). sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.content:
The landscape of software engineering is undergoing a fundamental shift, driven by the increasing use of Large Language Model (LLM) agents capable of autonomously generating code (Wang et al., 2025; SWE-agent Team, 2025; Yang et al., 2024). These agents have demonstrated remarkable proficiency in 'shallow' generation tasks, where objectives are broad and requirements are loosely defined (Qwen Team, 2026; OpenAI, 2026; Hong et al., 2024; Kimi, 2026). This flexibility is well suited to a range of development scenarios, such as rapid prototyping, demo applications, frontend interfaces, and proof-of-concept implementations, where structural decisions can be left to the agent. However, this permissiveness becomes a liability when the target is a production-grade backend. Such systems must satisfy functional and non-functional requirements by exposing endpoints that adhere to API contracts, conform to architectural patterns, integrate with databases, and operate through designated ORM layers. The impact of these constraints on agent performance remains largely unexplored.

sections.heading: 2 Related Work
sections.content:
Greenfield app generation. Recent benchmarks have begun to evaluate LLM agents on generating entire apps from scratch, yet none adequately captures the challenges of constrained multi-file, repository-level backend development. Luo et al. (2026) measure output against existing test suites from well-known libraries but reward unconstrained generation from under-specified prompts. Seo et al. (2026) target repository generation for reproducing research papers, while Zhao et al. (2025) provide skeleton libraries for agents to complete. Ding et al. (2025) evaluate coding agents on repository generation from reverse-engineered natural-language specifications of Python codebases. Neither targets backend systems nor systematically varies the degree of structural constraint. Vero et al. (2024) is closer to our setting, tasking LLMs with generating backend services from OpenAPI specifications across multiple frameworks and languages, with evaluation through end-to-end functional and security tests. However, it targets single-file solutions via direct prompting rather than multi-file, repositories generated through agentic interaction, and does not study how layering architectural constraints affects generation quality.

summary.summary_text: This paper presents a systematic empirical study of LLM agent performance on backend code generation under varying degrees of structural constraints. The researchers evaluated agents on 80 greenfield and 20 feature-implementation tasks across 8 web frameworks using an OpenAPI-based evaluation framework with end-to-end behavioral tests and static verifiers. Key findings identify a "constraint decay" phenomenon where agent performance declines substantially as structural requirements accumulate, with capable configurations losing 30 points on average in assertion pass rates. Framework analysis reveals significant disparities: agents perform better on lightweight, explicit frameworks like Flask than on convention-heavy environments like FastAPI and Django. Error analysis identifies data-layer defects, including incorrect query composition and ORM runtime violations, as the primary failure mode. The work highlights that joint satisfaction of functional and structural requirements remains a significant open challenge for coding agents.
summary.general_claim: LLM agents' performance on backend code generation degrades significantly as structural constraints accumulate, with framework-specific sensitivities and data-layer defects being key failure modes.
key_findings: Constraint decay phenomenon: capable agents lose approximately 30 points in assertion pass rates when structural requirements accumulate
Framework sensitivity: agents perform better on explicit frameworks (Flask) than convention-heavy ones (FastAPI, Django)
Data-layer defects are the leading cause of failures: incorrect query composition and ORM runtime violations
Systematic evaluation across 80 greenfield plus 20 feature-implementation tasks spanning 8 web frameworks
OpenAPI-based methodology decouples functional correctness from structural compliance assessment

claims.validity_basis: averaged across 8 capable configurations over multiple runs, no CIs reported
claims.evidence_basis: computed average across 8 model-agent configurations with 3 runs per task

claims.validity_basis: definitional claim set by the authors
claims.evidence_basis: follows directly from study design definition

claims.text: A% scores on the 16-task representative subset correlate with full 80-task results at Pearson r = 0.98 and Spearman rho = 0.95 (p < 10^-12, N = 24), validating the subset evaluation strategy.
claims.validity_basis: statistical correlation computed on 24 paired observations with high significance

claims.validity_basis: directly reported benchmark numbers
claims.evidence_basis: 3 independent runs per task for this configuration

claims.validity_basis: directly reported result on 16-task subset
claims.evidence_basis: measured on 16-task subset with 3 runs per task

claims.validity_basis: directly reported numeric results
claims.evidence_basis: single configuration benchmark number on 16-task subset

claims.text: The large and consistent gap between A% and pass@1 underscores that LLM agents still lack the cross-file consistency and constraint adherence needed for deployment without manual intervention.
claims.validity_basis: interpretive conclusion supported by consistent pattern across all configurations
claims.evidence_basis: observed across all model-agent configurations in Table 2

claims.validity_basis: matched-pair design isolates this effect from other constraints
claims.evidence_basis: matched-pair analysis reported in Table 3a across all model-agent configurations

claims.validity_basis: matched-pair result, causal mechanism is interpretive
claims.evidence_basis: matched-pair design in Table 3a isolating the architecture constraint

methods.name: Constraint Decay Evaluation Pipeline
methods.description: This paper introduces an evaluation methodology that holds a fixed OpenAPI specification constant while systematically varying structural constraints (architecture, database, ORM) across backend generation tasks, using dual evaluation with end-to-end behavioral tests and static verifiers to isolate the effect of structural complexity.

methods.name: Architecture Verifier
methods.description: This paper introduces a static verifier that enforces the Clean Architecture constraint by checking for the presence of at least three of four canonical layer directories and detecting upward dependency violations via import statement analysis across Python and JavaScript source files.

methods.name: Database Verifier
methods.description: This paper introduces a static verifier that scans source lines using regex patterns to confirm the prescribed database engine (SQLite or PostgreSQL) is used and no alternative engine is present, excluding lock files from the scan.

methods.name: ORM Verifier
methods.description: This paper introduces a static verifier that detects whether the designated ORM (SQLAlchemy for Python or Sequelize for Node.js) is used rather than raw SQL, by scanning source files for ORM-specific import patterns and constructor calls.

methods.name: Behavioral Test Suite
methods.description: This paper introduces a unified stateful HTTP behavioral test suite comprising 32 requests covering 19 API endpoints and 291 assertions, implemented as a Postman collection executed via Newman to evaluate all implementations against the RealWorld Conduit OpenAPI specification regardless of internal code structure.

methods.name: Assert% (A%) Metric
methods.description: This paper introduces the Assert% metric, defined as the mean fraction of behavioral test assertions passed across all runs of a given configuration, used as the primary evaluation axis because it captures partial progress more stably than the all-or-nothing pass@1.

methods.name: Codebase Ablation
methods.description: This paper introduces a method for constructing feature implementation tasks by applying git diff patches to remove entire feature verticals (routes, controllers, services, data-access code, and model definitions) from open-source RealWorld repositories, producing tasks that require an agent to re-implement the missing functionality.

methods.name: Mini-SWE-Agent
methods.description: This paper uses Mini-SWE-Agent from prior work (SWE-agent Team, 2025) as one of two agent scaffolds: a minimal approximately 100-line Python scaffold interacting with the environment exclusively through bash commands, with a re-aligned system prompt injected to steer it toward a generative pipeline.

methods.name: OpenHands
methods.description: This paper uses OpenHands from prior work (Wang et al., 2025) as one of two agent scaffolds: a full-featured agent framework providing dedicated tools for file editing, terminal execution, code search, and task tracking, with a custom termination criterion introduced to enforce complete evaluation trajectories.

methods.name: Clean Architecture
methods.description: This paper uses the Clean Architecture pattern (Martin, 2017) from prior work as one of three structural constraint dimensions, requiring code to be organized into four layers (routes/handlers, services/use cases, models/entities, repository/data access) with strict top-down dependency direction.

methods.name: OpenAPI 3.0
methods.description: This paper uses the OpenAPI 3.0 specification format from prior work as the standardized machine-readable functional requirement for all tasks, enabling unambiguous endpoint definitions and framework-agnostic behavioral test generation.

methods.name: Behavior-Driven Development (BDD)
methods.description: This paper uses Behavior-Driven Development (North et al., 2006) from prior work as the methodological inspiration for its evaluation approach, applying the principle of holding functional specifications constant while varying non-functional requirements and testing against behavioral contracts rather than implementation details.

novelty.reasoning: The paper explicitly names a gap not addressed by prior work: no existing benchmark systematically layers non-functional structural constraints (framework, architecture, database, ORM) to measure their cumulative effect on LLM agent performance. The closest prior work, Vero et al. (2024), uses OpenAPI specs but targets single-file direct prompting rather than multi-file agentic generation with no constraint layering. SWEBench and its extensions address issue resolution in existing codebases, not greenfield constrained generation. The named phenomenon of 'constraint decay' (a 30-point average A% drop from L0 to L3) and the framework sensitivity axis (25-32 pp gap between lightweight and convention-heavy frameworks) are empirically grounded and non-obvious. However, the contribution is fundamentally an evaluation and benchmarking study built on existing agent scaffolds (Mini-SWE-Agent, OpenHands) and an existing API spec (RealWorld Conduit), and the core methodology of using OpenAPI specs plus behavioral tests is borrowed from Vero et al. - the novelty lies in the constraint-layering design and the resulting empirical findings rather than in a new technique or algorithm.

reproducibility.reasoning: The paper describes its methodology in substantial detail: verifier logic is specified in appendices C.1-C.3 (regex patterns, import analysis, directory checks), the behavioral test suite is a concrete Postman/Newman collection with 32 requests and 291 assertions against a public OpenAPI spec, prompt templates are in appendix E, and the execution pipeline has step-by-step walkthroughs in appendix I. The agent scaffolds (OpenHands, Mini-SWE-Agent) are both from prior public work, and the benchmark tasks are claimed to be open-sourced. However, HAS_CODE is False with no repository URL confirmed, several evaluated models are frontier API models (GPT-5.2, MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5) that require proprietary access, and critical operational details such as random seeds for the k=3 sampling, hardware specifications, and dependency/container versions are absent. An engineer could reimplement the evaluation framework from the appendix descriptions with moderate effort, placing this squarely in the partial-reproduction band.
missing: Public GitHub repository URL containing evaluation code, verifier implementations, and the Postman collection
Random seeds used for the k=3 independent sampling runs underlying pass@1 estimates
Hardware and infrastructure specifications (GPU type, count, memory) for the agent execution environment
Exact API version identifiers and endpoint configurations for closed models (GPT-5.2, MiniMax-M2.5, Kimi-K2.5)
Dependency versions or container image for the execution environment (Python version, Newman version, ORM library versions)
Confirmed public URL for the 80 greenfield and 20 feature-implementation task artifacts

trustworthiness.summary: The paper comes from a credible research group led by Paolo Papotti, a verified EURECOM professor with recent peer-reviewed publications at SIGMOD and NAACL in directly adjacent LLM and data management research. The two methodological claims (four constraint dimensions and the 3-of-4 layer threshold for the architecture verifier) are confirmed verbatim in the paper text. The headline quantitative finding of a 30-percentage-point drop has no independent numeric corroboration yet, which is expected for a preprint from May 2026, but the qualitative constraint decay phenomenon is broadly validated by practitioner commentary on Hacker News.

requirements.name: docker
requirements.rationale: Containerizes each agent-generated backend and the PostgreSQL service for isolated, reproducible test execution. OpenHands also runs its agent loop inside Docker.

requirements.name: postgresql
requirements.rationale: The database constraint (L2/L3 tasks) specifies PostgreSQL 16 as the required engine. The database static verifier checks generated code for correct PostgreSQL driver and connection usage.

requirements.name: newman
requirements.rationale: CLI runner for the Postman collection implementing the RealWorld Conduit behavioral test suite. Produces the assertion pass-rate (A%) scores central to all reported results.

requirements.name: nodejs
requirements.rationale: Runtime required for Newman and for JS-based target frameworks such as Hono and Sequelize that generated backends may use. The paper specifies Node.js 20.

requirements.name: openai
requirements.rationale: Python client for calling GPT models used as coding agents and as the LLM-as-Judge evaluator. litellm can serve as a unified proxy to also reach the MiniMax and Qwen endpoints evaluated in the paper.

requirements.name: openhands
requirements.rationale: Primary coding-agent framework evaluated in the paper; drives multi-file backend generation across all constraint levels and all eight framework targets.

requirements.name: swe-agent
requirements.rationale: Basis for the Mini-SWE-Agent configuration, the second agent evaluated in the paper. Required to reproduce the weaker-configuration results and constraint-decay comparisons.

requirements.name: sqlalchemy
requirements.rationale: The ORM constraint (L3 tasks) targets SQLAlchemy; the ORM static verifier checks generated Python backends for correct model definitions and query composition.

requirements.name: flask
requirements.rationale: One of the eight target web frameworks; the paper singles out Flask as a minimal, explicit framework where agents succeed most. FastAPI and Django (convention-heavy) are also required for the full benchmark suite and the framework-sensitivity analysis.

requirements.name: scipy
requirements.rationale: Provides Pearson r and Spearman rho correlation functions used to validate the 16-task subset against the full 80-task results, and the matched-pair statistical tests for per-constraint effect sizing.

requirements.name: pandas
requirements.rationale: Aggregates per-task evaluation results (A%, pass@1, verifier outcomes) across agent configurations, framework targets, and constraint levels for analysis and figure generation.

requirements.name: git
requirements.rationale: Used in the codebase-ablation method to snapshot and diff generated multi-file repositories across constraint levels, enabling isolated comparison of individual constraint effects.
